appraisal_events.evidence: Grief revives at a syllable — "comme ces mourants chez qui le cerveau ne pense plus et dont on fait se contracter un membre en y enfonçant une aiguille"; he seeks out occasions of jealousy to keep her; a novel by Bergotte, a map of France, the name of Tours act on him like "substances vénéneuses", and the chain ending at Chaumont strikes "un choc si cruel que dès lors je ne pensais plus qu'à me garer contre la douleur".
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage stages the narrator as wholly at the mercy of a jealousy that outlives its object: he cannot read, cannot look at a map, cannot dream without being wounded, and is reduced to shielding himself rather than living.

appraisal_events.evidence: In the dream she promises she has done nothing wrong and has only kissed Mlle Vinteuil on the lips, and he concludes "elle devait recommencer à mentir comme au temps où elle niait tout"; the association to the Buttes-Chaumont, where she had claimed never to have been, still convicts her; and she is finally described as "une fille probablement pareille à toute autre" for whose effect "n'importe quelle autre femme eût pu servir".
appraisal_events.explanation: The dead Albertine is lowered twice over in the narration's ledger: settled into as a liar whose guilt is now the working assumption, and denied any personal distinction in the force she exerted, which is credited to a tangle of the narrator's own habits.

status_effects.explanation: He suffers without defence or control, courting pain to keep the memory and then flinching from names on a map; the dead woman still governs his days.
The passage's verdict on her falls: a liar assumed guilty even in dreams, and a girl probably like any other whom any other woman could have replaced.

ambiguities: The dream confession that most incriminates Albertine is explicitly authored by the narrator himself — "c'est moi-même qui les avais prononcées" — so her posthumous guilt in this passage rests on evidence he manufactures.
